Chapter 4: Intersectionality—How Race, Class, Gender, and Sexuality Intertwine.
Life’s never just about one thing, is it? We’re all shaped by so many forces—race, class, gender, sexuality, and more. These aren’t just separate threads; they’re woven together, often in ways we don’t even notice until they bump up against each other.
If you want to really understand racism, you’ve got to see how these different threads intersect. They create challenges and even opportunities that are totally unique to each person.
Picture a college student on a mostly white campus. Not only are they Black, but they’re also the first in their family to go to college, and they identify as queer. Each part of who they are brings its own set of expectations—and hurdles. Sometimes, they feel like they’re carrying the weight of representing their entire race. In other moments, their sexuality is brushed aside or just ignored completely. And if they struggle with classes? People are quick to blame their background, instead of looking at whether the school’s really giving them the support they need.
Most folks don’t see how different types of discrimination can actually pile on top of each other. For example, take something as simple as a standardized test for college admissions. On the surface, it might seem totally fair. But if you dig a little deeper, you’ll see it can hit students very differently depending on where they come from. If you’ve had great schools and all the resources, you’re more likely to do well. If not, you’re left behind. So, a policy that looks neutral? In reality, it just makes existing inequalities even worse.
And it’s not just about race or class. Gender and sexuality play a huge role too. Think about it—a Black woman deals with different challenges than a Black man. And both face things that a white woman might not. For a queer person of color, they might feel left out in both LGBTQ spaces and communities of color. These overlapping identities don’t just shape the discrimination folks experience—they also shape their resilience.
Understanding intersectionality means we have to look past the easy answers. It means asking, who actually benefits from this policy? And who’s being left out? It means realizing that fighting racism also means standing up against sexism, homophobia, and classism. All these struggles are connected—and so are the solutions.
And this isn’t just some academic theory. It’s something people live every day, through the choices they make and the policies they support. Like, if a workplace only gives parental leave to mothers, it reinforces old gender roles and even racial stereotypes. Or think about a health clinic that ignores LGBTQ patients—the people who might need care the most end up pushed aside.
So, the work of antiracism? It’s not just about race. It’s about creating a world where everyone actually gets a fair shot, no matter where they come from. That means really listening to people whose experiences are different from your own—and being ready to change the rules and habits that leave folks out or do them harm. It’s a journey of learning, and sometimes unlearning, of seeing things with fresh eyes.
